summary.text: The Quran commands the acts of wudu in 5:6 but never mentions a resolve in the heart, so the question turns on the hadith 'Actions are only by intentions' and on how the jurists classified wudu itself. Three of the four schools, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali, make the intention obligatory, while the Hanafis hold it is a sunna and not a condition. All four agree that the intention is an act of the heart and is never spoken aloud.

paragraphs.text: The verse of wudu commands four acts on named limbs and says nothing about a resolve in the heart, which is why Ibn Rushd treats it as the basic text for the acts of wudu rather than for its conditions. The Companions and early scholars focused on the opening words: Zayd ibn Aslam and Ata' ibn Yasar read 'when you rise to prayer' as rising from the night's sleep, a reading Malik records in the Mudawwana and Ibn Qudama cites in al-Mughni. The Hanafis read the verse as carrying no indication at all that intention is a condition, a point Ibn Abidin attributes to Ibn Kamal's commentary on al-Hidaya. Ibn Uthaymeen turned the same verse into a question, does the command require an intention for the wudu itself or only for the prayer, and answered that one should intend compliance with Allah's command in every wudu, whether for prayer, tawaf, reciting Quran or dhikr.

The hadith on which the majority build is the first in al-Bukhari, 'Actions are only by intentions,' reported by Umar and graded authentic and agreed upon (al-Bukhari 1, Muslim 1907). Islamweb explains the majority's use of it: what the hadith denies without an intention is the legal status and the reward of the act, not its outward form. Two further reports are used to show that wudu is itself an act of worship rather than mere cleaning: Thawban's hadith, 'Be upright, though you will never be able to do so fully... and none but a believer maintains his ablution,' graded sound on the criterion of Muslim by Shu'ayb al-Arna'ut, and argued from on the grounds that an act only a believer perseveres in must be worship; and the report 'there is no wudu except from a sound or a smell' (Musnad Ahmad 10093), graded sound by Shu'ayb al-Arna'ut, with a parallel wording in Musnad Ahmad 8944.

The naming formula produced a separate cluster. 'There is no wudu for one who does not mention the name of Allah over it' appears in Sunan al-Darimi 688 with no grade given in the text cited, in Musnad Ahmad 11370 graded sound through other chains by Shu'ayb al-Arna'ut, and in Jami' at-Tirmidhi 25 graded hasan by Shakir, al-Albani, Bashar Awad and Zubair Ali Zai, alongside Ahmad ibn Hanbal's remark that he knew no hadith on the topic with a good chain. The Hanbali school places the intention at this very moment, at the first obligation, which for them is the tasmiyah. Most directly relevant to the question is a statement of the successor Rabi'ah ibn Abi Abd al-Rahman, recorded by al-Darawardi and graded sound as a maqtu report (Abu Dawud 102): the meaning of 'no wudu for one who does not mention the name of Allah over it' is the person who washes and bathes without intending wudu for prayer or a bath for sexual impurity, a successor's interpretation, not the Prophet's words.

The Companions' own practice is described at length without any spoken formula. Uthman's wudu, narrated by Humran, is graded sound (Sunan an-Nasa'i 84) and hasan by Shu'ayb al-Arna'ut in Musnad Ahmad 436; in both he performs the washing, then says this is the wudu of the Messenger ﷺ, and no uttered intention appears in the description. The report on the authority of Ibn Umar, 'no prayer is accepted without purification,' is graded sound in Tirmidhi 1 and Ibn Majah 272, and establishes the link between purification and prayer without addressing intention.

The Hanafis hold the intention to be a sunna, not a condition: prayer is valid with such a wudu, and leaving the intention is a slight sin. Ibn Abidin says prayer is valid 'with us' by a wudu even if not intended, that the intention is prescribed so the act becomes worship and a cause of reward, and that wudu and the lifting of hadath are not termed worship because they do not depend on it; the Mabsut of Shaykh al-Islam is quoted that the commanded wudu is not achieved without intention, but the validity of prayer does not depend on it, since the aim is purity and water purifies by its nature. The school makes intention obligatory in tayammum, because tayammum is not purifying in itself, and holds the obligatory limbs to be only the face, forearms, feet and a quarter of the head.

The Malikis count the intention as an obligation and as the seventh fard. Al-Dasuqi says the seventh obligation is the intention, which is the aiming at the thing, and its place is the heart; it is the intention of lifting the hadath at the washing of the face, or at the first obligation if he begins elsewhere. The same intention and continuity are obligatory in ghusl as in wudu.

The Shafi'is make the intention an obligation and the first of six. Al-Nawawi says the obligations are six, the first being the intention, which is obligatory in purifications from hadath, though not in removing physical impurity, and al-Sharbini lists the same six. One may make the intention at the washing of the hands with the basmala, or at the face; the simple intention of wudu or of the obligatory wudu suffices. It must be present to the mind, mere awareness not sufficing, and one intends lifting the lesser hadath, or purity for prayer, or purity for what is unlawful without it; it is obligatory not to intend cutting it and not to commit a nullifier such as apostasy, and one may distribute the intention across the limbs. Intending cooling or cleaning along with a valid intention does not harm it.

The Hanbalis hold the intention to be a condition, with no wudu, ghusl or tayammum valid without it. Ibn Qudama says it is a condition for purification from hadath, reported from Ali and held by Rabi'ah, Malik, al-Shafi'i, al-Layth, Ishaq, Abu Ubaydah and Ibn al-Mundhir, while al-Thawri and the people of opinion held it unnecessary in water purification. Al-Buhuti says intending an absolute wudu does not lift the hadath, because wudu is sometimes habit and sometimes worship, so it needs the intention to distinguish it; it must be made at the first obligation, the tasmiyah, and must be maintained, meaning one does not intend to cut it. Intending what wudu is prescribed for but not required, such as recitation, dhikr, adhan, sleep or anger, does lift the hadath.

Ibn Rushd locates the root of the disagreement precisely: whether wudu is pure worship whose only meaning is nearness to Allah, like prayer, or a rationally understood purification like washing away physical filth. Whoever saw it as pure worship required the intention; whoever saw the meaning as the removal of impurity did not. That is why the Hanafis can say the water purifies 'by its nature' and the intention is needed only for reward, while the majority answer that the Prophet ﷺ attached reward and expiation to wudu, which makes it an independent worship, and an independent worship needs an intention.

The second reconciliation is over what 'actions are only by intentions' negates. The majority read it as denying validity and legal status without intention; the Hanafis read it as denying reward and acceptance, not validity, and hold the verse silent on the point. Ibn Uthaymeen rejected the Hanafi comparison with removing physical impurity as an analogy with a differentiating factor, since wudu is a rewarded act that expiates sins whereas removing a substance is achieved by any means.

The third is internal to the Hanafi position and often missed: the same school makes the intention obligatory in tayammum and not in wudu, reasoning that tayammum is not purifying in itself and so needs to be designated, while water does purify by nature. So the Hanafi view is not a blanket denial of intention in purification. The fourth narrows the whole dispute: IslamOnline observes that intention in the sense of the heart's resolve hardly leaves a Muslim who is performing wudu for prayer at all, asked what he is doing, he says he is performing wudu, not cleaning himself, and the disagreement bites only in the rare case of someone who washed to cool down and then decided to pray. On the related hadith, 'there is no wudu except from a sound or a smell,' the soundest reading given is that it concerns what obliges wudu, not what validates it.

Even among the three schools that require it, the content differs, which shows the disagreement is about definition as much as evidence: the Malikis specify the intention of lifting the hadath at the face, the Shafi'is accept the bare intention of wudu or of purity for prayer and allow it to be split across the limbs, and the Hanbalis hold that a merely absolute wudu intention lifts nothing. What no school disputes is that the intention is an act of the heart and that no spoken formula is transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ or his Companions.

IslamOnline's fiqh section states that the majority, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, al-Layth and others, make the intention a fard, citing the hadith of intentions and its restrictive particle innama, and notes that Ibn al-Qayyim answered the Hanafis in I'lam al-Muwaqqi'in with fifty-one points. Islamweb answers the same question by saying the intention is a condition for wudu's validity, supported by the Sunnah.

On the wording, the fatwas are firm and uniform. Ibn Baz calls verbalising the intention in prayer and wudu an innovation not transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ or his Companions, since its place is the heart, and IslamQA records the consensus of the imams that it need not be uttered. Al-Albani calls the spoken formula idle talk that is not permissible, and notes that a man standing at the tap does not need to announce what he is about; he also held a wudu valid where a man dived into the sea intending wudu, provided he rinsed his mouth and nose, without a fixed sequence. Ibn Uthaymeen says the spoken intention is contrary to the Prophet's guidance, and that it is enough to have it in the heart without vocalising.

Two further answers address anxiety around the topic. AMJA (Dr. Salah al-Sawi) says the intention accompanies the acts of wudu, so that one has present in mind that he intends wudu and is not merely washing to clean or cool. AMJA (Dr. Muwaffaq al-Ghalayini) says a general intention before beginning suffices, and that a person with continuous incontinence needs no special intention beyond it. Ibn Uthaymeen told a questioner whose scrupulosity had him repeating wudu that a sane person is always aware of what he is doing, and the Permanent Committee ruled that merely intending to renew a wudu does not invalidate the first one.
